summary: Diabetes mellitus is chronic hyperglycemia from too little insulin, too little insulin effect, or both. Boards ask you to separate type 1 from type 2, read the diagnostic cutoffs, tell diabetic ketoacidosis from hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state, and trace how high glucose damages vessels, nerves, kidneys, eyes, and lenses.

points: Type 1: T cell mediated autoimmune destruction of beta cells, so insulin deficiency is absolute.
Type 1 markers: HLA-DR3 and HLA-DR4, autoantibodies to GAD65, insulin, IA-2, and ZnT8.
Type 1 symptoms appear after most beta cells are gone; onset is usually in childhood or young adulthood, in thin patients.
Type 2: insulin resistance in muscle, fat, and liver plus progressive beta cell failure.
Type 2 islets show amyloid deposits made of amylin (islet amyloid polypeptide).
Type 2 is tied to obesity (especially visceral fat), inactivity, and family history; twin concordance is higher than in type 1.
Type 1 is ketosis prone; in type 2, the remaining insulin usually holds back lipolysis and ketone production.

Diabetes if any one is met: fasting glucose at least 126 mg/dL, 2-hour glucose at least 200 mg/dL on a 75 g oral glucose tolerance test, HbA1c at least 6.5%, or random glucose at least 200 mg/dL with classic symptoms.
Without symptoms, an abnormal result is confirmed with a repeat test.
Prediabetes: fasting 100 to 125 mg/dL, 2-hour 140 to 199 mg/dL, or HbA1c 5.7 to 6.4%.
HbA1c is hemoglobin that glucose has attached to nonenzymatically, so it rises with average glucose.
Red cells live about 120 days, so HbA1c reflects about the last 3 months.
HbA1c reads falsely low when red cells turn over fast (hemolysis, recent blood loss).
DKA: with no insulin, lipolysis runs unchecked; high glucagon then drives the liver to turn the fatty acids into beta-hydroxybutyrate and acetoacetate.
Ketoacids cause an anion gap metabolic acidosis; deep, rapid Kussmaul breathing blows off CO2 to compensate.
DKA also brings fruity (acetone) breath, abdominal pain, vomiting, and dehydration from osmotic diuresis.
Serum potassium is often high in DKA because insulin lack and hyperosmolality shift potassium out of cells, yet total body potassium is low from urinary loss.
HHS: usually older type 2 patients; glucose often above 600 mg/dL and osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg cause severe dehydration and confusion or coma.
HHS has little or no ketosis because a small amount of insulin is enough to block ketogenesis.
Advanced glycation end products (AGEs) form when glucose binds proteins without enzymes; they cross-link collagen and trap LDL and albumin in vessel walls.
AGEs binding their receptor (RAGE) trigger inflammation, oxidative stress, and growth factor release, thickening basement membranes.
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis: plasma proteins leak into small arteriole walls, giving a pink, glassy, narrowed lumen.
Polyol pathway: aldose reductase turns glucose into sorbitol in tissues that take up glucose without insulin (lens, nerves, retina, kidney).
Sorbitol is trapped and pulls in water (osmotic injury); the reaction uses NADPH, leaving less glutathione to fight oxidants.

Results: the polyol pathway gives cataracts (lens) and peripheral neuropathy (Schwann cells and nerves); AGEs and vessel injury speed up atherosclerosis, leading to MI, stroke, and peripheral artery disease.
Any 3 of 5: abdominal obesity, triglycerides at least 150 mg/dL, low HDL (under 40 mg/dL in men, under 50 mg/dL in women), blood pressure at least 130/85 mm Hg, fasting glucose at least 100 mg/dL.
Waist cutoffs (US): over 102 cm (40 in) in men, over 88 cm (35 in) in women.
Insulin resistance is the common thread: visceral fat floods the liver with free fatty acids, so the liver makes more VLDL (high triglycerides, low HDL).
Acanthosis nigricans: velvety dark plaques in the neck folds and axillae; high insulin stimulates IGF-1 receptors on keratinocytes and fibroblasts.

tricks.label: The potassium paradox
tricks.text: In DKA the lab shows high potassium while the body is short of it. Insulin pushes potassium back into cells, so serum potassium falls fast once insulin is given.

tricks.label: Insulin-independent tissues get sorbitol
tricks.text: Lens, nerves, retina, and kidney take up glucose without insulin, so high blood glucose floods them and aldose reductase makes sorbitol. That list matches the classic chronic complications.

tricks.label: A little insulin stops ketones
tricks.text: It takes far less insulin to block lipolysis and ketogenesis than to move glucose into muscle. Type 2 patients keep that small amount, so they drift into HHS instead of DKA.

highYield: HbA1c reflects about 3 months of glucose because red cells live about 120 days.
DKA: anion gap metabolic acidosis, Kussmaul breathing, high serum potassium with total body depletion.
HHS: glucose often above 600 mg/dL, osmolality above 320 mOsm/kg, altered mental status, little ketosis.
Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules (nodular glomerulosclerosis) are highly characteristic of diabetic nephropathy; GBM thickening is the earliest change.
Albuminuria is the earliest clinical sign of diabetic nephropathy.
Aldose reductase converts glucose to sorbitol in lens and nerve, causing cataracts and neuropathy.
Type 2 islets show amyloid from amylin; type 1 islets show insulitis.
Acanthosis nigricans in an obese patient points to insulin resistance.
pitfalls: A normal or high serum potassium in DKA does not mean body stores are normal; they are depleted.
A urine dipstick for ketones detects acetoacetate, while beta-hydroxybutyrate is the main ketone in DKA, so the dipstick can underestimate ketosis.
Hyaline arteriolosclerosis occurs in both diabetes and hypertension; in diabetes it affects efferent as well as afferent arterioles.
Type 2 diabetes can present in obese teenagers, and type 1 can present in adults, so use antibodies and ketosis, along with age.

summary: A thyroglossal duct cyst is a leftover piece of the tract the thyroid follows as it descends from the tongue to the neck. Boards test where it sits, why it moves when the patient swallows or sticks out the tongue, how it differs from a branchial cleft cyst, and why the surgeon checks for a normal thyroid before removing it.

points: The thyroid starts as an endodermal outgrowth at the foramen cecum, between the front two-thirds and back third of the tongue.
It descends in the midline in front of the pharynx, the hyoid bone, and the laryngeal cartilages, reaching its final spot by about week 7.
It stays connected to the tongue by the thyroglossal duct, which normally disappears.
A pyramidal lobe is a normal remnant of the lower end of the duct.
If part of the duct persists, its lining secretes fluid and forms a cyst anywhere along the path.
Most common congenital neck mass; usually found in childhood, sometimes in adults.
Painless, smooth, midline mass, most often at or just below the hyoid bone.
Moves upward with swallowing (tied to the hyoid and larynx) and with tongue protrusion (tract runs to the tongue base).
Lined by respiratory or squamous epithelium; thyroid follicles may sit in the wall.
Complications: infection from mouth bacteria through the tract, abscess, a draining sinus or fistula, and rarely papillary thyroid carcinoma in the cyst.
Usually from the second branchial cleft (persistent cervical sinus).
Sits on the lateral neck along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid, below the angle of the jaw.
Does not move with swallowing or tongue protrusion.
Can also become infected, often after an upper respiratory infection.
If the thyroid stopped descending, the mass may contain the only functioning thyroid tissue (ectopic thyroid).
Removing it would leave the patient permanently hypothyroid.
Neck ultrasound or a thyroid scan confirms a normally placed gland before surgery.
Standard surgery removes the cyst, the whole tract, and the middle of the hyoid body (Sistrunk procedure) to prevent recurrence.

rows: Lateral, anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid

tricks.label: Middle moves, side stays
tricks.text: A midline neck lump that rises when the patient sticks out the tongue is a thyroglossal duct cyst. A lump on the side, along the front edge of the sternocleidomastoid, that stays put is a branchial cleft cyst.

tricks.label: Follow the thyroid's trip
tricks.text: Trace the path from the foramen cecum down past the hyoid to the lower neck. A thyroglossal duct cyst or ectopic thyroid tissue (such as a lingual thyroid) sits somewhere on that midline path.

highYield: Midline neck mass that moves up with swallowing and tongue protrusion: thyroglossal duct cyst.
The thyroid arises from the foramen cecum at the base of the tongue.
Infection is the most common complication, because the tract connects to the mouth.
Confirm a normally located thyroid before removal; the mass may be the only thyroid tissue.
Lateral neck cyst at the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid: branchial cleft cyst.
The pyramidal lobe is a normal remnant of the thyroglossal duct.
pitfalls: Moving with swallowing alone also happens with thyroid nodules; moving with tongue protrusion points to the thyroglossal tract.
A midline lump below the hyoid is not always a cyst; ectopic thyroid tissue looks the same, so image the neck first.
Branchial cleft cysts are lateral and do not rise with swallowing or tongue protrusion; position is the fastest way to tell the two apart.

Final position below the cricoid cartilage by about week 7
Thyroglossal duct normally disappears
Pyramidal lobe is a remnant of the lower duct
Cyst is most often at or just below the hyoid
Lingual thyroid forms if descent fails

summary: The anterior pituitary depends on a low-pressure portal blood supply, so a sudden drop in blood flow can kill it. Boards test Sheehan syndrome after postpartum hemorrhage, why the posterior lobe is spared, which hormones are lost, and pituitary apoplexy, sudden bleeding into an adenoma.

notes.h: Why the anterior pituitary is vulnerable
points: The anterior pituitary gets most of its blood from the hypophyseal portal veins, a low-pressure system fed by the superior hypophyseal arteries.
The posterior pituitary has a direct arterial supply from the inferior hypophyseal arteries, so it is usually spared.
In pregnancy, estrogen-driven lactotroph hyperplasia enlarges the anterior pituitary, raising its oxygen demand without a matching rise in blood supply.
Severe postpartum hemorrhage causes hypotension and vasospasm, and the enlarged anterior lobe infarcts.
Necrosis must destroy most of the anterior pituitary before symptoms appear.
Onset can be right after delivery or months to years later.
Diabetes insipidus is uncommon because the posterior lobe usually survives.
Low prolactin: failure to breastfeed, often the first sign.
Low FSH and LH: amenorrhea (menses do not return) and infertility.
Low ACTH: fatigue, hypotension, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia; no hyperpigmentation and usually no hyperkalemia because aldosterone runs on renin-angiotensin.
Low TSH: cold intolerance, weight gain, constipation, slow reflexes.
Low GH: hypoglycemia tendency and reduced muscle mass.
Loss of axillary and pubic hair from low adrenal and ovarian androgens.
Sudden hemorrhage or infarction into a pituitary adenoma, often a macroadenoma no one knew about.
Sudden severe headache from rapid expansion and meningeal irritation.
Visual loss, often bitemporal, from compression of the optic chiasm above.
Ophthalmoplegia from compression of the cavernous sinuses beside the sella (CN III, IV, VI).
Acute loss of ACTH causes adrenal crisis with shock and hypoglycemia; glucocorticoids are life-saving.
Triggers include anticoagulation, head trauma, pregnancy, and surgery.

tricks.label: Portal means vulnerable
tricks.text: The anterior lobe drinks second-hand, low-pressure portal blood, so it dies when pressure drops. The posterior lobe has its own arteries and keeps releasing ADH.

tricks.label: Start with the baby
tricks.text: A new mother who cannot breastfeed after a big bleed is the classic opening. Then work down the hormone list: no periods, no thyroid hormone, no cortisol, no body hair.

highYield: Failure of lactation after severe postpartum hemorrhage: Sheehan syndrome.
Posterior pituitary is spared because it has a direct arterial supply; diabetes insipidus is uncommon.
Pregnancy enlarges the anterior pituitary through lactotroph hyperplasia.
Secondary adrenal insufficiency causes no hyperpigmentation and usually no hyperkalemia.
Sudden headache, visual loss, and ophthalmoplegia in a patient with a pituitary adenoma: apoplexy.
Pituitary apoplexy causes acute adrenal crisis, which is the main threat to life.
pitfalls: Sheehan is ischemic and painless; apoplexy is sudden and painful with mass effect.
Primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison disease) gives hyperpigmentation and hyperkalemia; pituitary causes do not.
Ophthalmoplegia means lateral spread into the cavernous sinus, while bitemporal hemianopia means upward pressure on the chiasm.
Postpartum amenorrhea alone can be normal during breastfeeding; failure to lactate is what points to the pituitary.

dumps.p: Draw the hypothalamus, pituitary stalk, and both pituitary lobes. Label the arteries and the portal system, and mark which lobe dies in Sheehan syndrome and why.

Hypophyseal portal veins carry blood down the stalk
Anterior lobe receives mainly low-pressure portal blood
Inferior hypophyseal arteries supply the posterior lobe directly
Pregnancy enlarges the anterior lobe through lactotroph hyperplasia
Hypotension after hemorrhage infarcts the anterior lobe
Posterior lobe and ADH are usually spared

summary: Endocrine tumors show up on the exam either by the hormone they make or by the space they take up. You need to recognize the main adrenal, pancreatic, parathyroid, pituitary, and thyroid tumors, the MEN syndromes that link them, pheochromocytoma, and the endocrine paraneoplastic syndromes.

points: Cortical adenoma: small, well circumscribed, yellow; most are nonfunctional incidentalomas, some make cortisol or aldosterone.
A cortisol-secreting adenoma suppresses ACTH, so the rest of that gland and the other gland atrophy.
Cortical carcinoma: rare, large, invasive, often functional and virilizing; poor prognosis.
Metastases (lung, breast) to the adrenal are more common than primary adrenal carcinoma.
Neuroblastoma: adrenal medulla tumor of children under about 5, from neural crest; N-MYC amplification predicts a worse outcome.
Neuroblastoma shows Homer Wright rosettes, raises urine HVA and VMA, and can cause opsoclonus-myoclonus.
Insulinoma: beta cell tumor, usually small, single, and benign; the most common functional islet cell tumor.
Whipple triad: hypoglycemic symptoms, low plasma glucose, and relief when glucose is given.
Insulinoma gives high insulin and high C-peptide during hypoglycemia; C-peptide is cut from proinsulin in equal amounts.
Injected insulin gives high insulin with low C-peptide, because commercial insulin has no C-peptide and it suppresses the patient's own release.
Glucagonoma (alpha cell): hyperglycemia, necrolytic migratory erythema, weight loss.
Somatostatinoma (delta cell): diabetes, gallstones, steatorrhea, achlorhydria, because somatostatin blocks insulin, CCK, pancreatic enzymes, and gastrin.
Parathyroid adenoma: about 85% of primary hyperparathyroidism; one enlarged gland of chief cells, other glands normal or shrunken.
Parathyroid hyperplasia involves all four glands and is the pattern in MEN1 and MEN2A.
Parathyroid carcinoma is rare; very high calcium, a firm neck mass, and invasion or metastasis define it.
Pituitary microadenoma is under 1 cm; macroadenoma is 1 cm or larger.
Prolactinoma is the most common functional pituitary adenoma; prolactin suppresses GnRH.
Nonfunctioning macroadenoma: bitemporal hemianopia (crossing nasal fibers in the chiasm), headache, hypopituitarism, mild hyperprolactinemia from stalk compression.
Craniopharyngioma: suprasellar tumor from Rathke pouch, calcified and cystic with oily fluid; causes headache, bitemporal hemianopia, diabetes insipidus, and growth failure in children.
Follicular adenoma and follicular carcinoma look alike on cytology; only capsular or vascular invasion on the removed nodule proves carcinoma.
Follicular carcinoma spreads through blood to bone and lung.
Papillary carcinoma is the most common thyroid cancer, linked to childhood radiation; it spreads by lymphatics to cervical nodes, with excellent prognosis.
Medullary carcinoma comes from calcitonin-secreting C cells; its amyloid stroma is made from calcitonin; RET mutations link it to MEN2.
Anaplastic carcinoma: older adults, rapidly growing invasive mass with dysphagia and hoarseness, TP53 mutations, nearly always fatal.
Euthyroid (nontoxic) diffuse or multinodular goiter: normal TSH, compression causes dysphagia, dyspnea, or stridor.
A cold nodule (no radioiodine uptake) carries a higher cancer risk than a hot nodule, though most cold nodules are still benign.
Pheochromocytoma: chromaffin cell tumor of the adrenal medulla that makes catecholamines.
Episodic headache, palpitations, and sweating with hypertension that can be sustained or come in spells.
Diagnose with raised plasma free metanephrines or 24-hour urine metanephrines.
Associated with MEN2A, MEN2B, von Hippel-Lindau disease, and neurofibromatosis type 1.
Small cell lung carcinoma can secrete ACTH (Cushing syndrome) or ADH (SIADH with hyponatremia).
PTH-related peptide from squamous cell lung carcinoma or renal cell carcinoma causes hypercalcemia with suppressed PTH.

tricks.label: MEN1 = 3 P's, MEN2A = 2 P's, MEN2B = 1 P
tricks.text: MEN1: pituitary, parathyroid, pancreas. MEN2A: parathyroid and pheochromocytoma (plus medullary thyroid). MEN2B: pheochromocytoma only (plus medullary thyroid, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus).

tricks.label: C-peptide tells you who made the insulin
tricks.text: The pancreas releases insulin and C-peptide together. High insulin with high C-peptide means the body made it (tumor or sulfonylurea); high insulin with low C-peptide means it came from a syringe.

tricks.label: Papillary goes by lymph, follicular goes by blood
tricks.text: Papillary carcinoma spreads to neck nodes. Follicular carcinoma invades vessels and lands in bone and lung, which is why vascular invasion is what proves follicular carcinoma.

highYield: Most common thyroid cancer: papillary carcinoma, with Orphan Annie eye nuclei and psammoma bodies.
Medullary thyroid carcinoma: C cells, calcitonin, amyloid stroma, RET, MEN2.
Follicular carcinoma is diagnosed by capsular or vascular invasion and spreads by blood.
Insulinoma: high insulin and high C-peptide during hypoglycemia; think MEN1.
Most common functional pituitary adenoma: prolactinoma.
Child with a calcified suprasellar mass and diabetes insipidus: craniopharyngioma.
Pheochromocytoma: episodic headache, sweating, palpitations; raised metanephrines; MEN2, VHL, NF1.
Hypercalcemia with low PTH in a smoker: PTH-related peptide from squamous cell lung carcinoma.
pitfalls: Fine needle aspiration cannot separate follicular adenoma from follicular carcinoma; the whole capsule must be examined.
Mild hyperprolactinemia with a large pituitary mass is usually stalk compression; a prolactinoma that size makes far more prolactin.
Neuroblastoma and pheochromocytoma both come from the adrenal medulla; neuroblastoma is a childhood tumor with HVA and VMA, pheochromocytoma is mostly an adult tumor with raised metanephrines.
Parathyroid adenoma is one big gland; hyperplasia (as in MEN) is all four.
Hypercalcemia of malignancy has suppressed PTH; primary hyperparathyroidism has high or inappropriately normal PTH.

Papillary histology: Orphan Annie eye nuclei, nuclear grooves, psammoma bodies
Papillary spreads by lymphatics to cervical nodes; excellent prognosis
Follicular: capsular or vascular invasion, blood spread to bone and lung
Medullary: C cells, calcitonin, amyloid stroma
Medullary: RET mutations, MEN2A and MEN2B
Anaplastic: older adults, TP53, rapid local invasion, very poor prognosis

dumps.p: Draw three body outlines labeled MEN1, MEN2A, and MEN2B. Mark the tumors of each syndrome on the right organ and write the gene under each outline.

MEN1: pituitary adenoma, often prolactinoma
MEN1: pancreatic endocrine tumors such as gastrinoma and insulinoma
MEN1 gene encodes menin, a tumor suppressor
MEN2A: medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, parathyroid hyperplasia
MEN2B: medullary thyroid carcinoma, pheochromocytoma, mucosal neuromas, marfanoid habitus
MEN2A and MEN2B: RET gain-of-function mutation

summary: Two infections hit endocrine glands hard enough to show up on the exam. Acute suppurative thyroiditis is a rare bacterial infection of the thyroid that usually leaves hormone levels normal, and Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome is bilateral adrenal hemorrhage in overwhelming sepsis, classically meningococcemia, that causes shock from acute adrenal insufficiency.

points: Rare because the thyroid has a capsule, a rich blood and lymph supply, and high iodine content.
Usual organisms: Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus pyogenes, Streptococcus pneumoniae, and mouth anaerobes; fungi and mycobacteria in immunocompromised hosts.
Routes: blood or lymph spread, direct spread from the neck, or a piriform sinus fistula (left side, often recurrent in children).
Risk: preexisting thyroid nodules or goiter, immunosuppression, recent fine needle aspiration.
Fever, sudden anterior neck pain, a hot, red, tender thyroid lobe, and pain on swallowing.
Thyroid function is usually normal; leukocytosis and raised ESR are common.
Complications: abscess, spread into deep neck spaces or mediastinum, airway compromise, sepsis.
Bilateral massive hemorrhage into the adrenal glands during overwhelming sepsis.
Classic cause is Neisseria meningitidis, a gram-negative diplococcus; other causes include Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Pseudomonas, and staphylococci.
Meningococcal lipooligosaccharide (endotoxin) drives TNF and IL-1 release, endothelial injury, and DIC.
DIC forms microthrombi and consumes platelets and clotting factors, so the adrenals bleed and infarct.
Loss of cortisol removes vascular tone support (cortisol lets vessels respond to catecholamines), so shock does not respond to fluids alone.
Loss of aldosterone adds salt wasting, hyponatremia, and hyperkalemia.
Usually a child or young adult with fever that progresses over hours.
Petechial rash that spreads into purpura (purpura fulminans) from DIC and vessel damage.
Hypotension and shock, hypoglycemia, hyponatremia, hyperkalemia.
Labs: low platelets, prolonged PT and PTT, low fibrinogen, high D-dimer.
Risk: terminal complement deficiency (C5 to C9), asplenia, crowded living such as dormitories.
Very high mortality; survival needs antibiotics plus glucocorticoid replacement.

charts.title: Painful thyroid: infectious vs subacute granulomatous thyroiditis
rows: Follows a viral illness, often low-grade fever
One lobe hot, red, sometimes fluctuant

charts.title: Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: cause to finding
rows: Vessels stop responding to catecholamines; salt wasting

tricks.label: Hot lobe, normal labs
tricks.text: A febrile patient with one red, hot, tender thyroid lobe and normal thyroid hormone levels points to bacterial thyroiditis. Painful thyroiditis with abnormal levels and low radioiodine uptake points to subacute granulomatous thyroiditis.

tricks.label: Rash plus shock that will not lift
tricks.text: Fever, a spreading purpuric rash, and hypotension that fluids and pressors cannot fix suggest the adrenals are gone. Think meningococcemia with Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome.

highYield: Acute suppurative thyroiditis: fever, painful tender thyroid lobe, normal thyroid function, risk of abscess.
Recurrent left-sided suppurative thyroiditis in a child suggests a piriform sinus fistula.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: bilateral adrenal hemorrhage in sepsis, classically Neisseria meningitidis.
Meningococcal endotoxin triggers DIC, which drives the adrenal hemorrhage and the purpuric rash.
Shock in Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome resists treatment until cortisol is replaced.
Terminal complement (C5 to C9) deficiency raises the risk of Neisseria infections.
pitfalls: Painful thyroid with normal hormone levels favors infection; painful thyroid with thyrotoxicosis and low uptake favors subacute thyroiditis.
Waterhouse-Friderichsen is acute primary adrenal failure; Sheehan syndrome is pituitary failure causing secondary adrenal insufficiency.
Neisseria meningitidis endotoxin is lipooligosaccharide, which lacks the long O-antigen chains of the lipopolysaccharide on enteric gram-negative rods.
Hyperkalemia here comes from aldosterone loss in primary adrenal failure; pituitary causes spare aldosterone.

Petechial rash progressing to purpura

dumps.p: Make a table comparing acute infectious thyroiditis and subacute granulomatous thyroiditis: cause, onset, how the gland feels, thyroid function, radioiodine uptake, and complications.
l: Infectious: bacteria such as Staphylococcus aureus and streptococci
Subacute: follows a viral illness
Infectious: one lobe hot, red, sometimes fluctuant
Infectious: thyroid function usually normal
Subacute: transient thyrotoxicosis with low radioiodine uptake
Infectious risk: piriform sinus fistula, nodular goiter, immunosuppression
Infectious complication: abscess and deep neck spread
